book.title: The Medieval Origins of the Legal Profession: Canonists, Civilians, & Courts

argument.statement: Renewed interest in Roman law and the rise of canon law in the Western church triggered consolidations that required formal training and helped legal advocacy become professional by 1250.

book.rationale: The book primarily explores the historical development of the legal profession from ancient Rome through the medieval period, focusing on the intersection of law and church authority.
book.summary: In the aftermath of sixth-century barbarian invasions, the legal profession that had grown and flourished during the Roman Empire vanished. Nonetheless, professional lawyers suddenly reappeared in Western Europe seven hundred years later during the 1230s when church councils and public authorities began to impose a body of ethical obligations on those who practiced law. James Brundage’s The Medieval Origins of the Legal Profession traces the history of legal practice from its genesis in ancient Rome to its rebirth in the early Middle Ages and eventual resurgence in the courts of the medieval church. By the end of the eleventh century, Brundage argues, renewed interest in Roman law combined with the rise of canon law of the Western church to trigger a series of consolidations in the profession. New legal procedures emerged, and formal training for proctors and advocates became necessary in order to practice law in the reorganized church courts. Brundage demonstrates that many features that characterize legal advocacy today were already in place by 1250, as lawyers trained in Roman and canon law became professionals in every sense of the term.
